problem.title: Solving GraphQL N+1 Queries with DataLoader
problem.prompt: A mobile app release adds a `seller { rating }` field to the Order History screen, issuing `orders(first: 50) { id items { qty product { id title seller { id name rating } } } }`. Your Apollo/Java GraphQL Gateway resolves each field independently: 1 query for 50 orders -> 50 queries for items -> 200 queries for products -> 200 gRPC calls for sellers = **451 backend calls per HTTP request**. At just 60 mobile RPS, backend traffic surges to **27,060 QPS**, saturating PostgreSQL and `Seller-Service` and causing 503s. Redesign the GraphQL execution layer to bound backend queries and protect against arbitrary nested queries.

spark.summary: A single nested GraphQL query (`orders(first: 50) { items { product { seller { rating } } } }`) triggers 1 + 50 + 200 + 200 = 451 sequential DB/gRPC calls per HTTP request, saturating PostgreSQL at just 60 RPS.
spark.keyTakeaway: Always pair request-scoped `DataLoader` batching (collapsing N+1 into `WHERE id IN (...)`) with GraphQL query depth/complexity limits and persisted query allowlists.

**Core Mechanics:** GraphQL lets mobile clients compose arbitrary nested selections like `orders(first: 50) { items { product { seller { rating } } } }`.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts 451 Sequential Calls Collapsed to 4 Batched Tier Calls (Mobile Client -> GraphQL + DataLoader -> Postgres (Orders/Items) -> Seller gRPC); Complexity Gate -> Per-Tick DataLoader -> Batched Backends (Complexity & Depth Gate -> Request DataLoaders -> Postgres (ANY($1)) -> Seller-Service BatchGetSellers(ids)).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Three common mistakes break naive DataLoader rollouts: **Singleton / Shared DataLoader**: Sharing a `DataLoader` across requests leaks User A's cached data to User B and serves stale mutations. Reduce 451 calls to `<= 4` batched calls while blocking abusive queries: **Request-Scoped `DataLoader` per Tier**: Instantiate `OrderItemsLoader`, `ProductLoader`, and.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Request-scoped batching and complexity governance are mandatory in modern BFFs: **GraphQL Federation & Subgraphs**: Prevents subgraph N+1 fanout across microservices.

learningJourney.title: Database connection exhaustion and unbounded recursive query DoS
learningJourney.explanation:
Without batching and query governance, one mobile release triggers two failures:

1. **110x Backend QPS Amplification**: `60 RPS` of mobile screen loads generates `27,060` DB/gRPC calls/sec.
2. **Cyclic Query DoS**: Malicious or accidental cyclic queries (`order -> items -> product -> seller -> orders -> ...`) exhaust gateway CPU and DB pools.

learningJourney.title: Why singleton DataLoaders and un-chunked IN() clauses break
learningJourney.explanation:
Three common mistakes break naive DataLoader rollouts:

- **Singleton / Shared DataLoader**: Sharing a `DataLoader` across requests leaks User A's cached data to User B and serves stale mutations.
- **Partial Coverage**: Adding a `SellerDataLoader` while forgetting `OrderItemsDataLoader` still leaves a `51x` N+1 at tier 2.
- **Unbounded `maxBatchSize`**: Passing `> 65,535` bind parameters in a single PostgreSQL `IN (...)` fails; chunk batches (e.g., `maxBatchSize=500`).
learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Why singleton DataLoaders and un-chunked IN under real concurrency or scale.

learningJourney.title: Enterprise solution: Request-Scoped DataLoader + Complexity Limits
learningJourney.explanation:
Reduce 451 calls to `<= 4` batched calls while blocking abusive queries:

- **Request-Scoped `DataLoader` per Tier**: Instantiate `OrderItemsLoader`, `ProductLoader`, and `SellerDataLoader` per HTTP request so in-request deduplication never bleeds across users. Use `WHERE id = ANY($1)` (Postgres) and `BatchGetSellers(ids)` (gRPC) with `maxBatchSize=500`.
- **Query Complexity & Depth Limits**: Reject queries with depth `> 6` or complexity score `> 1,000` (where list arguments like `first: 50` multiply child cost) *before* execution.
- **Persisted Query Allowlists (APQ)**: In production, accept only SHA-256 registered query hashes from mobile clients.

learningJourney.title: Where DataLoader batching powers federated APIs
learningJourney.explanation:
Request-scoped batching and complexity governance are mandatory in modern BFFs:

- **GraphQL Federation & Subgraphs**: Prevents subgraph N+1 fanout across microservices.
- **BFF Aggregation Layers**: Batches product, pricing, and inventory lookups for mobile screens.
- **ORM Lazy-Loading Prevention**: Replaces per-row lazy JPA/SQLAlchemy fetches with explicit batch loaders.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why MUST a GraphQL `DataLoader` instance be created per-request rather than shared as a global singleton?

options.text: DataLoader caches resolved keys in memory; sharing it across requests leaks user data and serves stale state after mutations
options.feedback: Correct: DataLoader's built-in memoization map is designed strictly for single-request deduplication.

options.text: Global DataLoaders cannot call gRPC BatchGet endpoints
options.feedback: The transport works either way, but cross-request caching causes security and staleness bugs.

options.text: GraphQL depth limits only apply to singleton DataLoaders
options.feedback: Query depth/complexity validation runs at parse/validation time before resolvers.

_problemQuestions.prompt: A user edits their bio and refreshes the page, only to see the old bio for 2 seconds because the read hit a lagging replica. Which consistency guarantee was violated?

options.explanation: Read-Your-Writes ensures a client always observes its own completed writes.
The write was durable on the primary; the replica simply lagged.
Atomicity governs all-or-nothing commit, not cross-replica visibility.

_problemQuestions.prompt: Why does placing `request_timestamp` at the very beginning of a 3,000-token system prompt hurt latency and cost?

options.explanation: BPE still tokenizes the text normally.

options.text: It invalidates prefix/KV caching for all subsequent 3,000 tokens on every request
options.explanation: Correct! Prefix KV caching requires an exact token match from index 0 onward.
Output length is unaffected; Prefill cache reuse is what breaks.
